pedagogy.summary: Universal gravitation reframes gravity from 'the force that makes things fall down on Earth' to a universal attractive force acting between ALL objects with mass, everywhere — the same force that pulls an apple down also holds the Moon to Earth and the planets to the Sun. Two ideas do the heavy lifting at KS3. First, orbits: an orbiting body is not 'balancing' or 'free of gravity' — it is continuously falling toward the central body, but moving sideways fast enough that it keeps missing, so its path curves into a closed loop (Newton's cannonball). Second, weight vs field strength: weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g), mass is invariant but g differs between planets, so the same astronaut weighs less on the Moon though their mass is unchanged. The most damaging misconception — 'there is no gravity in space' — must be tackled head-on: astronauts float not because gravity is absent (it is nearly as strong in orbit) but because they and their spacecraft are in continuous free fall together. Newton's thought experiment (cannon on a mountain, faster and faster) is the canonical bridge from projectile to orbit.
bestPractices: Teach the orbit as 'falling sideways' using Newton's cannonball: fire a projectile faster and faster from a mountaintop until it falls all the way around — making orbit continuous with everyday falling rather than a separate phenomenon
Confront 'no gravity in space' directly: contrast the near-full strength of Earth's gravity at the ISS with the free-fall explanation for weightlessness (everything falling together)
Separate mass from weight relentlessly with weight = mass × g: compare a fixed mass's weight on Earth, Moon, and Jupiter to show g — not mass — is what changes
Stress universality: the SAME attractive force operates between an apple and Earth, Earth and Moon, Sun and planets — scaling with mass — so gravity is not special to Earth's surface
Use predict-then-observe with orbital speed: let students see that too slow spirals in, too fast escapes, and a 'just right' sideways speed gives a stable orbit
keyRepresentations: Newton's cannonball diagram/simulation (projectile speed increasing until the path closes into an orbit)
Free-body 'falling sideways' vector picture: velocity tangent to the orbit, gravity pointing to the central body, path curving
weight = mass × g comparison table across planets/Moon (same mass, different weight)
Two-mass attraction diagram showing the force acts on BOTH bodies (Sun–planet, Earth–Moon)
Free-fall / weightlessness illustration (astronaut and station falling together)
commonMisconceptions: There is no gravity in space / astronauts float because there is no gravity (they are in free fall; gravity in orbit is nearly as strong as at the surface)
Gravity only acts downward on Earth, or only large/special objects like planets have gravity (all masses attract all masses)
Mass and weight are the same thing / your mass changes on the Moon (mass is constant; only weight, = mass × g, changes)
Orbiting objects are 'balancing' gravity with an outward force, or gravity switches off in orbit (orbit is continuous free fall; the only force is inward gravity)
Gravity requires air / there is no gravity without an atmosphere
Heavier objects fall faster (in free fall, acceleration due to gravity is the same regardless of mass)

learn.summary: Reframe gravity from 'the force that makes things fall on Earth' to a universal attractive force acting between all masses everywhere — the same force pulling an apple down holds the Moon to Earth and planets to the Sun. Two strands do the KS3 heavy lifting: (1) orbits as 'falling sideways' (Newton's cannonball) — an orbiting body is continuously falling toward the central body but moving sideways fast enough to keep missing, so its path curves into a closed loop; and (2) weight vs field strength, weight = mass × g, where mass is invariant but g differs between planets. Tackle 'there is no gravity in space' head-on: astronauts float not because gravity is absent (in a low orbit like the International Space Station's it is still about 90% as strong as at the surface) but because they and their spacecraft are in continuous free fall together.

activities.title: Newton's cannonball: tune launch speed until it orbits
feedback: If a learner expects the orbiting ball to need an outward or balancing force, point out the only force shown is gravity pointing inward; the net force is not zero — it constantly changes the direction of motion.
If they think a faster ball should fly straight off immediately, show that gravity still curves its path — only beyond escape speed does it leave for good.
If they say the orbiting ball is 'weightless' or 'free of gravity', highlight that gravity is fully acting the whole time; that is exactly what bends the path.
activities.rationale: Orbit-as-falling-sideways is a dynamic cause–effect best discovered by tuning one variable and watching the trajectory respond, making the counterintuitive 'orbit is continuous falling' concrete. Newton's cannonball is the canonical bridge from projectile to orbit. A live simulation that holds the gravity state and recomputes the path each frame lets the learner find the critical speed themselves; predict-then-observe strengthens the reasoning. Offered as a proposed interaction, not an empirically validated one.
sourceClaims: MS-ESS1-2 asks students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS1-2, MS-LS1-2]; gravity holds the solar system and galaxies together and controls orbital motions (Kepler's laws are outside the boundary).

KS3 physics requires: gravity force and weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g), with g on Earth about 10 N/kg and different on other planets and stars; and that gravity forces hold the Earth–Moon and Earth–Sun systems (qualitative treatment).
learnerActions: Set a launch speed for a cannonball fired horizontally from the top of a tall mountain and predict where it will land before firing.
Fire at a gentle speed and watch it arc out and hit the ground a short distance away.
Nudge the speed higher repeatedly, observing the ball land further each time and the curve of its fall starting to echo the curve of the planet.
Find the critical speed at which the ball falls all the way around without reaching the ground and loops back — a stable orbit.
Push faster still to stretch the circle into an ellipse, then faster again until the ball escapes entirely.
In your own words, state what the ball is actually doing when it orbits (it is only falling — it is just going sideways fast enough to keep missing the Earth).
activities.intendedInsight: An orbit is continuous free fall: in this idealised model (no air resistance), the only force is gravity pulling inward, curving otherwise-straight sideways motion into a closed loop. Too slow and the ball arcs down and hits the ground; from the circular-orbit speed up to just below escape speed it orbits (a circle at first, then longer ellipses as speed rises); at or above escape speed it leaves for good. Orbit is continuous with everyday falling, not a separate phenomenon.

activities.title: Same mass, different weight: weight = mass × g across worlds
feedback: If a learner says the Moon astronaut has less mass, correct that mass is the same everywhere — only weight changes because g is smaller on the Moon.
If they confuse which quantity is in newtons, note weight is a force (N) found by multiplying mass (kg) by g (N/kg).

Check the arithmetic: a 40 kg mass weighs about 400 N on Earth (40 × 10); on the Moon, where g is about 1.6 N/kg, it weighs only about 64 N (40 × 1.6); on a hypothetical world with g half of Earth's it would weigh about 200 N. The half-g world is an illustrative example, not the Moon.
activities.rationale: Separating mass from weight relentlessly with weight = mass × g, comparing one fixed mass across Earth, Moon and Jupiter, targets the mass–weight conflation directly and shows g, not matter, is what changes. A live recolour/readout where the mass number stays fixed while the weight readout changes makes the distinction vivid.
sourceClaims: KS3 physics requires: gravity force and weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g), with g on Earth about 10 N/kg and different on other planets and stars; and that gravity forces hold the Earth–Moon and Earth–Sun systems (qualitative treatment).
learnerActions: Stand a fixed mass on a scale and read its weight on Earth.
Switch the planet selector to the Moon, then Jupiter, each time reading the new weight while noting the mass number never changes.

Using weight = mass × g (with g ≈ 10 N/kg on Earth), calculate the weight of a 40 kg mass on Earth; then work out its weight on the Moon using the Moon's g ≈ 1.6 N/kg, and compare with a hypothetical world of half Earth's g.
State explicitly what changed (weight, because g changed) and what stayed the same (mass, the amount of matter).
activities.intendedInsight: Mass (amount of matter) is invariant; weight = mass × g changes because gravitational field strength g differs between planets. The same astronaut weighs less on the Moon though their mass is unchanged.

activities.title: Free fall explains floating: drop the whole station
feedback: If a learner says 'there is no gravity in space', show the gravity indicator still on and recall that at the ISS gravity is roughly 90% of surface strength.
If they say gravity and speed 'cancel to zero force', point out the net force is not zero — the unbalanced inward gravity is what curves the path; zero net force would give a straight line.
Reinforce: everything in the station falls at the same rate together, so nothing feels its weight pressing down.
activities.rationale: 'No gravity in space' is the most damaging, documented misconception; contrasting near-full gravity in orbit with the free-fall explanation for weightlessness confronts it head-on. Seeing the station and astronaut fall together, with gravity shown as still acting, is intended to supply conviction a verbal claim may not.
sourceClaims: 'There is no gravity in space' and 'astronauts float because there is no gravity' are documented, persistent misconceptions; weightlessness in orbit is due to continuous free fall, not the absence of gravity.
learnerActions: Toggle the cannon-and-station into free fall and watch the astronaut inside floating.
Note that the gravity indicator shows gravity fully on the whole time — nothing has switched off.
Explain why the astronaut floats: they and the station are falling together, so there is nothing to press them against a floor.
Predict what path the station would follow if gravity really were zero (a straight line off into space, not a circle).
activities.intendedInsight: Astronauts float because they and their spacecraft are in continuous free fall together, not because gravity is absent — in a low orbit like the ISS's, gravity is about 90% as strong as at the surface. Gravity provides the centripetal (inward) force; remove it and the station would fly off in a straight line.

activities.title: Talk it through with an astronaut in orbit (Socratic dialogue)
feedback: If the learner insists gravity is absent, the character asks what path they would follow with no force at all — a straight line, not an orbit.
If they reach free fall, the character confirms gravity is supplying the inward pull that keeps the path curving.
activities.rationale: An in-role dialogue may help surface and challenge a child's reasoning Socratically about a verbal, sticky misconception. Offered as a complement to the simulation rather than a replacement; conviction about the geometry is also well supported by seeing the free-fall/orbit trajectory, so pair this with hands-on tuning. Dialogue is one proposed route, not a proven superior medium.
sourceClaims: 'There is no gravity in space' and 'astronauts float because there is no gravity' are documented, persistent misconceptions; weightlessness in orbit is due to continuous free fall, not the absence of gravity.
learnerActions: Pose the question to an in-role astronaut character: 'Is there gravity up here? Why do you float if gravity is still pulling you?'
Offer your own explanation and have the character probe it with follow-up questions.
Revise your reasoning toward: gravity is present and strong, and floating is because everything is in free fall together.
activities.intendedInsight: The 'no gravity in space' belief is verbal and sticky; articulating and defending reasoning aloud can help surface and challenge it. The goal is to replace 'gravity is absent' with 'we are falling around the Earth'.

activities.title: Universality: the same force everywhere
feedback: If a learner says 'only planets or big things have gravity', explain gravity acts between all masses; it is simply too weak to notice between small objects.
If they think gravity needs air, note gravity acts in the vacuum of space — it does not depend on an atmosphere.
If they think only one body is pulled, show the force diagram acting equally on both bodies.
activities.rationale: Stressing universality — the same force between apple–Earth, Earth–Moon, Sun–planet, scaling with mass — counters the belief that gravity is special to Earth's surface or to large/special objects, and that gravity requires air. A diagram showing the mutual pull on both bodies makes the symmetry concrete. The MS-ESS1-2 claim supports the cosmic-scale (Sun–planet/solar-system) aspect; the everyday-object and no-atmosphere points are standard physics not directly cited by a source.
sourceClaims: MS-ESS1-2 asks students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS1-2, MS-LS1-2]; gravity holds the solar system and galaxies together and controls orbital motions (Kepler's laws are outside the boundary).
learnerActions: Examine a two-mass attraction diagram showing the force acting on BOTH bodies (apple–Earth, Earth–Moon, Sun–planet).
State the common rule: every mass attracts every other mass; the pull is stronger for bigger masses and weaker the farther apart they are.
Explain why we do not notice the pull between two everyday objects (it is real but far too weak to feel), and why planets' pull is obvious (huge mass).
Decide whether gravity could act in a vacuum with no air, and justify the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Gravity is universal: the same attractive force operates between an apple and Earth, Earth and Moon, Sun and planets; it is stronger for larger masses and weaker at greater distances. It is not special to Earth's surface, does not require an atmosphere, and acts equally on both bodies in a pair.

activities.title: Check and consolidate: weight calculations and the orbit diagnostic
feedback: A learner saying 'there is no gravity up there' holds the dominant misconception; reteach that gravity at the ISS is ~90% of surface strength and floating is free fall together.
A learner saying 'gravity and speed cancel to zero force' misreads free fall; the net force is the unbalanced inward gravity constantly changing direction of motion.
A learner saying their mass changes on the Moon has the mass–weight conflation; mass is fixed, weight = mass × g changes with g.

A full response explains orbit as continuous free fall with gravity as the centripetal force, affirms gravity is universal, distinguishes fixed mass from g-dependent weight, and transfers to a different planet or orbit.
activities.rationale: An assessment tests weight = mass × g, universality, and the 'why do astronauts float?' misconception, checking rather than building intuition, so it is placed after the simulation. The two-tier design is discriminating because the first tier (does gravity exist up there) is silent — the reasoning tier separates the misconception from the mechanism; asking what KEEPS the station in orbit forces the causal account. Recognition-only items check answers but do not elicit the learner's own explanation, so the open prompt is retained.
sourceClaims: KS3 physics requires: gravity force and weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g), with g on Earth about 10 N/kg and different on other planets and stars; and that gravity forces hold the Earth–Moon and Earth–Sun systems (qualitative treatment).
learnerActions: Complete weight = mass × g calculations for a fixed mass on different planets (give the missing weight for Earth, Moon and Jupiter).
Answer the diagnostic: 'Astronauts on the Space Station float as if weightless. Does that mean there is no gravity up there? Explain what is really keeping the station in orbit.'

Give the two-part answer: there IS gravity (roughly 90% of surface strength at the Station), and floating is because the station and astronauts are in continuous free fall, with gravity supplying the inward (centripetal) force that curves their motion into an orbit.
Answer the probe: 'If gravity in orbit were really zero, what path would the Station follow — a circle or a straight line?' and justify (a straight line, because no force means no curving).
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidation: apply weight = mass × g numerically and articulate orbit as continuous free fall with gravity providing the centripetal force. Both 'no gravity' and 'gravity provides the orbit' predict floating, so the reasoning must be stated to distinguish them.

constraints: KS3 treatment is qualitative for orbital systems; Kepler's laws are outside the boundary. Use g ≈ 10 N/kg on Earth.
Address the 'no gravity in space' misconception explicitly — do not let a demonstration imply gravity switches off; always show gravity as still acting during free fall.

Make clear the net force on an orbiting body is not zero: there is no outward or balancing force. Gravity is the single unbalanced inward force; 'balanced forces in orbit' is itself a misconception to correct, not a model to teach.

When comparing weights across worlds, keep named bodies and their actual field strengths consistent (Earth g ≈ 10 N/kg, Moon g ≈ 1.6 N/kg); label any 'half-g' or round-number world as a hypothetical example so it is not confused with the Moon or Jupiter.

A static annotated cannonball figure or weight-vs-mass table is useful as a consolidation reference but does not let the learner tune orbital speed and watch the path respond; the manipulation is what builds the intuition, so treat static labelling as a scaffold, not the main activity.
Recognition-only quiz items check calculations and distractor-selection but do not elicit the learner's own causal explanation; include the open two-tier prompt so the reasoning is stated.

A 3D view can convey orbital planes and the Sun–planet–moon hierarchy but adds navigation cost; the core 'falling sideways' insight is a planar trajectory that reads clearly in 2D. Use 3D only when exploring how multiple orbits sit in space; this is a scope note, not a claim that 3D adds nothing.

Optional interaction examples (speed slider, planet selector with live weight readout, free-fall toggle, lift-the-flap 'why doesn't it fall down?' cards, in-role astronaut dialogue) are illustrative of the learning mechanism, not mandatory mechanisms or evidence of medium superiority.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original bestPractices described too-slow launches as spiralling in; for a dragless Newton's cannonball this is imprecise — a below-orbital projectile follows a suborbital ellipse and crashes into the ground. Corrected to 'arcs down and crashes into the ground' in the activity.

Independent review added the Moon's actual g ≈ 1.6 N/kg (~64 N for 40 kg) to the weight activity so the named Moon and the worked 'half-g = 200 N' example cannot be conflated; the half-g world is now explicitly labelled hypothetical.

Source row states gravity at the ISS is 'roughly 90%' (and elsewhere 'nearly as strong as') surface strength; this is approximate and altitude-dependent — retained as stated but flagged as an estimate.

The claim that weightlessness is due to free fall rather than absence of gravity is marked verified:false in the source (NASA/IOP-SPARK misconception guidance); treated as well-established physics but note the specific citation is unverified in the row.

No source[].claim directly supports the universality facets that gravity acts between everyday objects (too weak to notice) or in a vacuum with no air, nor the Moon's specific g value; MS-ESS1-2 supports only the cosmic-scale aspect. These are standard physics, not source-verified.

Legacy confidence was 'high'; not independently re-validated here. Comparative-efficacy framing in the original (that only a live simulator delivers conviction, that 3D 'adds nothing', that a quiz only assesses) has been softened to narrowly scoped affordances/limits, as catalog ratings do not establish necessity.
Self-audit of arithmetic: a 40 kg mass weighs ~400 N on Earth at g≈10 N/kg; ~64 N on the Moon at g≈1.6 N/kg; ~200 N on a hypothetical half-g world. These figures are correct as written.

probeDeeper: If gravity in orbit were really zero, what path would the Station follow — a circle or a straight line off into space? Why?
Newton imagined firing a cannonball faster and faster from a mountain until it never lands. What is it actually doing then?
Your mass is 40 kg here. On the Moon, does your mass change, your weight, or both? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: There IS gravity in orbit — at the Station's height it's roughly 90% as strong as at the surface. The astronauts float because they and the station are in continuous FREE FALL: gravity keeps pulling them toward Earth, curving their straight-line motion into an orbit — they are 'falling around' the Earth. Gravity provides the centripetal force; with no gravity they would fly off in a straight line, not orbit.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'there's no gravity in space — that's why astronauts float' (the dominant space-gravity misconception)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Gravity at the ISS is ~90% of surface strength; they float because they're in free fall, falling around the Earth together with the station.
errorPatterns.distractor: There is no gravity in space, so they float.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says orbit is weightless because gravity is absent up there

errorPatterns.pattern: 'an orbiting object floats because the forces are balanced / it has escaped Earth's pull' (misreads free fall as zero net force)
errorPatterns.nextMove: The net force is NOT zero — gravity is the unbalanced centripetal force constantly changing the direction of motion (Newton's cannonball).
errorPatterns.distractor: The station floats because Earth's gravity and its speed cancel out to zero force.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the station floats because gravity and its speed cancel to zero force

errorPatterns.pattern: 'gravity only acts between huge bodies — not between everyday objects' (gravity treated as non-universal)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Gravity is universal — every mass attracts every other; it's simply far too weak to notice between small objects.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: denies gravity acts between all masses; 'only planets have gravity'

errorPatterns.pattern: 'on a planet with weaker gravity your MASS is less — you'd have less matter' (mass–weight conflation)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mass (amount of matter) is fixed everywhere; weight = mass × g is what changes with gravitational field strength.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says mass changes when g changes

responseLevels.gap: Says there is no gravity in space; treats orbit as floating free of any force, or thinks mass changes with gravity.
responseLevels.full: Explains orbit as continuous free fall with gravity supplying the centripetal force that curves otherwise-straight motion, affirms gravity is universal (all masses attract), and distinguishes fixed mass from g-dependent weight across planets; transfers to a different orbit or planet.
responseLevels.partial: Knows gravity acts in orbit but describes floating as 'balanced forces' rather than free fall, or can't say why gravity curves the path into an orbit.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Astronauts on the Space Station float around as if weightless. Does that mean there is no gravity up there? … Explain what is really keeping the station in orbit.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 'No gravity in space' and 'gravity provides the orbit' both predict floating astronauts, so tier one is silent — the reasoning tier separates them. A child saying 'there's no gravity up there' holds the dominant misconception; one explaining free fall / gravity curving the path has the mechanism. Asking what KEEPS it in orbit forces the causal account: no force means a straight line, not a circle.
